Historical Resources

Applicable  historical  useinformation  will also be assessed  by a review  of four  or more  of the following:
Sanborn  Fire Insurance  Maps,  city  directorylistings,  topographic  maps,  aerial  photographs,  building
permits,  or other  available  historical  sources.  In addition,  Rincon  will review  previous  environmental  or
geotechnical  reports  conducted  at the subject  property,  if provided  by the City.

Site Reconnaissance

Rincon  will coordinate  with  the City to appropriately  access  the site and conduct  a reconnaissance  to
identify  obvious  potential  environmental  liabilities.  Immediately  adjacent  properties  (as accessible)  will be
visuallyinspected  from  public  thoroughfares.  Rincon  also provides  in-house  Unmanned  Aircraft  System
(UAS)/Drone  services  that  can utilized  forlarge  undeveloped  or difficult  to access  areas  to capture  high
resolution  aerial  imagery  that  can be reviewed  to identify  potential  environmental  liabilities.

Owner/Operator/Occupant  Interviews

Rincon  will interview  the current  site owner  or a designated  representative  of the site owner,  and/or
operators/occupants  (as identified  by the City) to obtain  additional  information  regarding  past and present
site  uses as they  may have affected  the subject  property.  The ownerinterview  will include  transmittal  of an
interview  questionnaire  to the above-referenced  individual.  Operator  and/or  occupant  interviews  will be
conducted  onsite  during  the site reconnaissance.  We may also interview  otherindividualsincluding  past
owners  of the subject  property  and adjacent  property  owners.

Local Government Interviews

Rincon  will interview  State  and/orlocal  environmental  health  and/or  fire department  regulatory  agency
representatives  to obtain  additional  information  regarding  onsite,  adjacent,  and nearby  past and present
release  sites  that  may have affected  the subject  property.  Local  government  interviews  will be conducted
via phone  and/or  email.

Evaluation/Report  Preparation

Rincon  will prepare  reports  in accordance  with  the requirements  of ASTM E1527-21.  The reports  wil
document  the information  and findings  of the research  conducted  in the above  tasks,  include  a series
of maps  identifying  existing  site and nearbyland  uses and provide  conclusions  regarding  the potential
presence  and impact  of environmental  site conditions.  The Phase  I ESA report  will be signed  by the
Environmental  Professional  and will include  the required  declaration  statement.

For reports  covering  large  areas,  Rincon  may also present  the data  in an ArcGIS  Web Application  that
allows  for the user to easily  view  the site boundaries,  adjacent  propertyland  uses,  areas  of potentia
environmental  concern  and quickly  access  detailed  additional  information  on items  of concern  in an
 nteractive,  interned-based  format.  The benefit  of using  an ArcGIS  Web application  allows  the technical
documentation  and data  to be located  in one place  for reference.  Further,  if the Phase  I ESA moves  to a
Phasell  ESA, the Phasell  ESA data  can be included  in the ArcGIS  Database  to build  upon the Phase  I ESA
allowing  one central  database  for the project  technical  reports  and spatial  data.

  The objective  of a Phasell  ESAis  to evaluate  the nature  and extent  of contamination  and to assess  the
  significance  of the contamination  relative  to established  threshold  levels or some other risk-based
  criteria.  Phase II ESAs will be developed  by the Phasell  ESA Lead in coordination  with the Principal
  Technical  Advisor,  who is a California-licensed  Professional  Geologist  and Certified  Hydrogeologist.  We
  understand  that a Phasell  ESA project  under this contract  mayinvolve  assessment  of soil, groundwater,
  soil vapor, and related  infrastructure  materials,  and/or  building  materials.

  Assessmentis  sometimes  conducted  in phases,  which  mayinclude  a preliminary  site assessment,  one
  or more subsequent  phases  of assessment,  periodic  monitoring,  risk assessment.  and an evaluation  of
  risk-based  cleanup  levels.  The assessments  also involve  working  within  established  regulatory  agency
  guidelines  for assessment  and reporting.  That said, Rincon approaches  Phasell  ESAs holistically;  we
  balance  the benefits  of a phased  approach  with the benefits  of optimizing  data collection  during  a single
  mobilization  to meet project  deadlines.  While each project  will be scoped.  developed,  and implemented
  consistent  with ASTM E1903-11. the City's needs, and relevant  site-specific  nformation,  our approach  to
  Phase II siteinvestigations  will include  the following  tasks.

  0uality AssuranceProject Plan(0APP)
  A OAPP is a document  that describes  the plan for collecting  and using environmental  information  and
  lays the foundation  of data quality  assurance  that will facilitate  key environmental  decision  making.  The
  0APP captures  the quality  assurance  steps to support  the project  plan which  includes  project  oversight
  and communication;  quality  control  of samples  by using standard  operating  procedures  for the collection
  and analysis  of the samples:  data checks  during  collection,  manipulation,  and presentation;  and the data
  evaluation  process.

  Rincon will prepare  a generic  OAPP based on templates  we've developed  on past projects  in collaboration
  with Enthalpy  Analytical.  LLC (Enthalpy),  our preferred  laboratory  for this project.  Coordination  with the
  laboratory  is essential  during  the 0APP process,  and we have sriccessfully  developed  EPA-approved  OAPPs
  with Enthalpy  in the past. The generic  0APP has a shelflife  of 5 years and can be applied  to multiple  sites
  under a single assessment  grant.  with the objective  of streamlining  the assessment  work. The generic
  0APP is anticipated  to include  the following  information:

  *  Project  Management  - Project  organization,  problem  definition,  project  description/timeline

  @  Measurement  Data Acquisition  - Sampling  and analytical  method  requirements,  methods,  and Standard
  Operating  Procedures  (SOPs): lab equipment  calibration  and corrective  actions;  sample  custody  and
  handling  requirements'  analytical  sensitivity  and project  criteria;  field and laboratory  quality  control
  requirements;  data management  and documentation

  *  [)ata Evaluation  - Field data evaluation,  laboratory  evaluation,  data usability  and project  evaluation

  We will begin preparing  this document  shortly  after  project  authorization.  such that the EPA review
  process  can commence  as soon as possible  to avoid project  delays.  In parallel  with EPA review  of the
  generic  OAPP, Rincon  will also engage the community  to avoid project  delays.

Health and Safety Plan

Prior to commencement  of the assessment,  a site-specific  health and safety  plan (HASP) will be prepared
by support  staff  and reviewed  by the Phase II ESA Lead and Program  Lead. For complicated  sites or site
with high levels of contamination,  an additional  review  may be performed  by Rincon's  in-house  Health  and
Safety  Manager,  pending  site conditions.  A site safety  meetiru:) will be held whereby  all field personnel  will
be informed  of possible  site conditions  and provided  with a copy of the HASP. During the field work,  daily
tailgate  meetings  will be held prior to the commencement  of each day's activities  and a copy of the HASP
will be onsite  at all times.  All site personnel,  subcontractors,  and visitors  who enter the site will be required
to sign the HASP form on a daily basis.

  SUBJECT:  RESOLUTION  APPROVING  MEMBERSHIP  IN  THE  GATEWAY  CITIES
  AFFORDABLE  HOUSING  TRUST

  PURPOSE:  To consider  joining  the Gateway  Cities  Affordable  Housing  Trust  ("Trust"),  a Joint
  Powers  of Authority  ("JPA")  formed  among  the cities  within  the Gateway  Cities  region  and
  created  for the purpose  of funding  housing  specifically  assisting  persons  and families  of extremely
  low, very  low,  low and moderate  income  within  the County  of Los Angeles.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider:
  a.  Authorizing  the City to join  the Gateway  Cities  Affordable  Housing  Trust;
  b.  Adopting  a Resolution  approving  the Joint Exercise  of Powers  Agreement  for the
  membership  to the Gateway  Cities  Affordable  Housing  Trust;  and
  c.  Authorizing  the Mayor  to execute  the Joint Powers  Agreement  with  the Gateway  Cities
  Affordable  Housing  Trust  in a form  acceptable  to the City Attorney.

  FISCAL  IMPACT:  There  is no financial  impact  expected  until  July 1, 2024.  Beginning  July  Y,
  2024, the estimated  membership  cost will  be $32,500,  annually.

  ANALYSIS:  Staff recommends  that the City join  the Trust,  a JPA formed  among  the cities within
  the Gateway  Cities  region.  The Trust provides  funding  to preserve  and produce  affordable  housing.
  These  funds  improve  the financial  viability  of individual  housing  projects  and programs.  This
  funding  can also increase  each project's  competitiveness  for additional  state and federal  funding
  sources.  Additionally,  the Trust  works  with  a variety  of government  and philanthropy  groups  to
  attract  more housing  funds to the Gateway  Cities  region.  Joining  the Trust  would  support  the City
  in achieving  the stated goals and objectives  of the 6th Planning  Cycle  2021-2029  Housing  Element
  Update  and supportthe  region  as awhole  to bring new dollars  to help fund more affordable  housing
  development.  To become  a member,  the City  Council  must adopt a Resolution  and authorize  the
  Mayor  to execute  the JPA with  the Trust.

  BACKGROUND:  The Gateway  Cities  region  of Los Angeles  County  includes  27 cities  located
  along the I-710  Corridor  in eastern Los Angeles  County.  Early  in 2021, the Gateway  Cities  Council

 Trust Membership
As outlined  in the JPA,  the Trust  does not build,  own,  or manage  housing  projects.  The  Trust
cannot  require  that housing  projects  be located  in specific  cities,  require  member  cities  to take an
allocation  of supportive  housing  units  or require  that cities  provide  a local  funding  match.  The
Trust  Board  of Directors  determines  whether  a funding  application  meets the Notice  of Funding
Availability  criteria.  Each  local  jurisdiction  maintains  land  use  control  and  processes  the
entitlement  consistent  with  its zoning  and municipal  code requirements.

The JPA  contains  a provision  that  requires  members  to contribute  towards  the administrative
expenses  of the Trust.  Member  cities  are not required  to contribute  :[unding  until  July  1, 2024.
Prior  to this period,  the GCCOG  has secured  administrative  formation  funding  for the Trust.  The
annual  membership  fees are based upon city population:

  a  Up to 30,000  =  $7,500
  -  30,001  to 60,000  =  $15,000
  -  60,001  tO  100,000  =  $32,500
  a  Greater  than 100,000  =  $47,500

This  amount  will  increase  annually  in an amount  equal  to the U.S.  Bureau  of Labor  Statistics
Consumer  Price  Index  for  Los  Angeles-Long  Beach-Anaheim  area for  the 12-month  period
preceding  the year the fees are assessed.

The City would  maintain  the right  to withdraw  from  the JPA subject  to an approved  resolution  and
by providing  a six-month  notice.

Governance
The  Trust  will  be a public  government  entity  established  by  a joint  powers  authority  and in
accordance  with  the Joint  Exercise  of Powers  Act,  as codified  in California  Government  Code
section  6500  et seq. The  Trust  will  be organized  to receive  public  and private  capital  and
administrative  funds to address local housing  needs. The Trust will  have an ongoing  administrative
revenue  source  from  city membership  fees as specified  in the Trust  Joint Powers  Agreement  (see
Attachment  B) to be signed  by each city that is a member  of the Trust.

The Trust  is governed  by a nine-member  Board  of Directors  ("Board").  Pursuant  to the Joint
Powers  Agreement  By-Laws  (Attachment  C), the Board  is comprised  of seven elected  officials
whose  governing  body  is a member  of the Trust  and appointed  by the Gateway  Cities  Council  of
Governments  Board.  A Trust  member  city  will  be represented  on the Board  by each population
category  specified  in the Trust  Membership  fee calculation.  Two  additional  Board  members  are
experts  in homelessness  or housing  policy  and  approved  by  the  Gateway  Cities  Council  of
Governrnents  City  Managers  Committee

Past and Future Pipeline of Affordable Housing Pro.iects
The Trust will  help cities in the Trust  subregion  address their Regional  Housing  Needs Assessment
(RHNA) which is mandated  by state housing  law as part of the periodic  process  of updating  local

 housing  elements  of the General  Plan for each city. RHNA  quantifies  the need for housing  within
each jurisdiction  during  specified  plaru'iing  periods.

In the past eight-year  plaru'iing  period,  from  2013 through  2021, the GCCOG  subregion  received
tax credit  funding  for 58 projects  totaling  nearly  6,000 housing  units.  A 2022  survey  of GCCOG
cities revealed  that there are 38 affordable  housing  projects  currently  in the pipeline  that have not
yet  started  construction.  Most  of  these  projects  need  critical  gap  subsidy  funding  to  start
construction.  These  38 pipeline  projects  would  benefit  from  additional  fiinding  provided  by the
Trust  which  could  accelerate  and facilitate  the creation  of an additional  4,000  affordable  housing
units in the COG  subregion.

 SUBJECT:  A REQUEST  BY VICE MAYOR  HURTADO  AND CITY COUNCIL  MEMBER
 BARRON  FOR CITY COUNCIL  TO DISCUSS WHETHER  THE CITY SHOULD  EXPLORE
 VIDEO/STREAMING  THE MEETINGS

 PURPOSE:  This item was continued from the Regular City Council Meeting of March 28, 2023
 and April 11, 2023 for the City Council to discuss whether its meetings should be video/streamed.

 RECOMMENDED  ACTION:  The City Council will consider if staff should present a project  and
 program that would permit the video/streaming of City Council meetings.

 FISCAL IMPACT:  This is a discussion item and development of direction, if any, to staff. Should
 City Council give direction to develop a project for the video/streaming of City Council meetingq,  then
 costs would be provided at that time as it relates to potential start-up and on-going costs for such a
 program.

 ANALYSIS:  Vice Mayor Hurtado and City Council Member Barron have requested this item  be
 placed on the agenda to allow the City Council to discuss its interest and whether direction should  be
 given  to staff.

 Attached  (Exhibit  A)  are the  results  of a quick  survey of neighboring cities to provide information
 related  to the  use of  cameras  to broadcast  their meetings.  While only four cities responded to the
 request,  it is recognized  that  nearly  all of the 14 cities asked do video/stream their Council meetings
 and/or  other  bodies.

 Based on the survey and other infoimation,  the act of providing video/streaming  of City Council
 meetings started for a large number prior to COVID and part of the local governrnent cable system
 agreements to provide public, educational, and governtnental (PEG) access channels. For many local
 governments, the process of providing video was to provide increase transparency of the legislative
 process and the only technology that existed to accomplish that goal. Around early 2012, technology
 became possible to allow ability to listen, see and participate in government process through platforms
 like Zoom and TEAMS.  These types of platforms grew significantly  as a result of COVID to allow
 not only the public but governmental officials that could not meet in person.

  l

  506
 For most  cities  that have been using  video/streaming,  they have a dedicated  staff member  or members
for the monitoring  and processing  of videos.  Even  a single  camera  usually  requires  an individual  to
monitor  and adjust  as the meeting  proceeds.  With  multiple  cameras,  the need for a dedicated  person  is
a necessity.  Supplementing  the  survey  are the personal  experiences  of the  City  Manager  in the
operations  of Monterey  Park  and Glendora,  which  have one to one and one-half  full-time  employees
operating  such programs.  The annual  staffing  costs are in excess of $125,000  for personnel  costs and

REPLENISHMENT  DISTRICT  PROPOSED RATE ADJUSTMENT  FOR FY 2023-24

PURPOSE:  To consider authorizing the Assistant City Manager/Director  of Public Works to
submit a Protest Letter to the Water Replenishment District ("WRD")  opposing the proposed
adjustment of the Replenishment Assessment for FY 2023-24.

RECOMMENDED  ACTION:  The City Council will consider authorizing the Assistant City
Manager/Director  of Public Works to submit a Protest Letter objecting to the proposed
Replenishment Assessment increase of $35 per acre-foot (approximately  8.5% for FY 2023-24)
by the Water Replenishment District.

FISCAL IMPACT:  The proposed water Replenishment Assessment by the Water WRD would
impact the Water Fund only. The full impact of the additional $35 per acre-foot is variable
depending on the amount of groundwater extracted during the fiscal year by the City. Based on
the previous year assessment, the increase would amount to approximately  an additional  $290,000.

ANALYSIS:  The City owns and operates a water system that uses groundwater as its primary
source. The water system extracts groundwater from the Central Basin Municipal Water District
groundwater aquifers which are regulated by the Water Replenishment District.  Groundwater
pumping has a rate which is known as the Replenishment Assessment ("RA").  The RA has a unit
cost per acre foot of water pumped that is currently set at $411 per acre-foot ("AF"), which the
WRD is proposing to increase by 8.5%. The City pumps an estimated 8,300 AF, annually;
therefore, the potential impact is $290,000 for FY 2023/24.

BACKRGO{JND:  The Southeast Water Coalition, of which Mayor Avalos sits as the City's
representative, has recommended to its members to file protest letters to the WRD relating to its
proposed water Replenishment Assessment increase for FY 2023-24.  The proposed increase of
$35 per acre foot on top of the existing $411 per acre-foot assessment would become effective on
July 1, 2023, unless 50% plus one of active pumpers object. There are sixty (60) active pumpers

 in the WRD service area, including the City of South Gate.  This means at least thirty-one  (31)
of those active pumpers must file a letter of protest to the WRD prior to May 2, 2023.

The proposed increase is much higher than the 3.1% that was recommended by the Finance and
Audit Committee of the WRD to its Board of Directors. It is also in conflict with the 0% increase
the WRD Budget Advisory Committee recommended to the WRD Board.

Should 50% plus one protest the proposed increase, the WRD would be prevented from
implementing the increase for the FY 2023-24. If less than the threshold file protest letters, the
WRD Board would be able to implement any increase up to the proposed $35 per acre-foot increase
to the existing $411 acre-foot assessment currently in place.

CITY OF SOUTH GATE
  REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING
  MINUTES
  TUESDAY, APRIL 25, 2023

  CALL TO ORDER  Maria del Pilar Avalos, Mayor called a Regular City Council Meeting to
  order at 6:51 p.m.

  INVOCATION  Steve Costley, Acting Director of Parks & Recreation

  PLEDGE OF
  ALLEGIANCE  Nicholas Iturriaga, Police Officer
  ROLL CALL  Yodit Glaze, City Clerk

  PRESENT  Mayor Maria del Pilar Avalos, Vice Mayor Gil Hurtado, Council Member
  Joshua Barron, Council Member Maria Davila, and Council Member Al
  Rios; City Treasurer Jose De La Paz, City Manager Chris Jeffers, City
  Attorney Raul F. Salina

  1
  COMMUNITY DEV/
  HOUSING  Following the conclusion of the Public Hearing, the City Council
  unanimously approved A, B & C by motion of Council Member Rios and
.  seconded by Council Member Barron:

  a.  Adopted Resolution No. 2023-20-CC entitled Resolution of the
  City Council of the City of South Gate, California, receiving and
  approving the Fiscal Year 2023-2024 Annual Action Plan;

  b.  Authorized the City Manager, or designee, to submit to the U.S.
  Department of Housing and Urban Development the Fiscal Year
  2023-2024 Annual Action Plan; and

  c.  Authorized the City Manager or his designee to enter into
  agreements with eligible subrecipients in a form acceptable to the
  City Attorney.

  ROLL CALL: Council Member Barron, yes; Council Member Davila,
  yes; Council Member Rios, yes; Vice Mayor Hurtado, yes; Mayor Avalos,
  yes.

  Meredith Elguira stated that Ms. Carol Averell will be presenting the item.

  Ms. Averell stated that each year an Annual Action Plan must be prepared
  with the five-year consolidated plan. This shows how the city will spend
  the allocations for CDBG and HOME Funding. The consolidated plan was
  adopted in 2020 and the FY 2023-2024 is the fourth year of the five-year
  consolidated plan.
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 25, 2023

1
COMMUNITY DEV/
HOUSING CONT'D  Ms. Averell stated that on March 8th a meeting with the Citizens' Advisory
  Committee was held and the committee and City staff made
  recommendations.

  Ms. Averell explained the chart.

  For Administration under CDBG we have a 20% cap. The total amount
  allocated for administration is $263,705. They are required to provide Fair
  Housing funding administration, so the recommendation is $24,000. The
  total amount for Program Administration and Planning is $239,705.

  For Public Service Grants we have a 15% cap. The total amount allocated
  is $197,779. The recommendation by the Citizen's Advisory Committee to
  Compatior Counseling Center is $25,000; $22,779 to Family Violence
  Prevention Program, $11,000 to South Gate Police Explorers; $9,000 to
  the Home Modification Program.

  For Non-Public Service which has no cap. We are recommending the
  remaining balance of $857,043. We are recommending $500,00 to the
  Commercial Façade Program; and $357,043 to start a Neighborhood
  Revitalization Grant Program.

  Ms. Averell stated that the additional recommendation from staff is to
  reallocate the $25,000 and split the amounts equally between Family
  Violence Prevention Program ($35,279) and South Gate Police Explorers
  ($23,500).

  For the HOME Funding Allocation, we received $740,613. This year there
  is an exception, there is a waiver that can be filed and request to use 20%
  of the entitlement for Administration which is $148,122. Allocating
  $80,000 for Affordable Housing Development (Azure Development 7916
  Long Beach Blvd) and $512,491 to the Affordable Housing Development
  for future projects.

  Mayor Avalos asked if anyone in the audience and zoom wished to speak
  on this item.

  Mario Dominguez, Jr., inquired if his mother could apply for the
  Neighborhood Revitalization Grant Program.

  Thomas Buckley is concerned the city is referring to and/or using an
  antiquated newspaper.

  Having no one else come forward, Mayor Avalos closed the audience
  portion.

  Page 2 of 12
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 25, 2023

1
COMMUNITY DEV/
HOUSING CONT'D  Meredith Elguira, Director of Community Development stated that for a
  resident to qualify for this program, the city would have to qualify them
  income-wise. There are other programs, and the city needs to appraise
  their homes to qualify for CDBG.

  City Attorney Salinas stated that the County of Los Angeles recognizes
  the Wave as a newspaper for general circulation.

  Council Member Barron asked if the Neighborhood Revitalization Grant
  Program is a new program.

  Ms. Elguira stated that yes, it is a new program.

  Council Member Barron asked if any publications have been posted.

  Ms. Elguira stated not yet because it requires Council approval first. And
  guidelines are required to be approved by HUD.

  Council Member Davila asked if any resident could apply.

  Ms. Elguira said yes.

  Vice Mayor Hurtado inquired about the total amount for the Graffiti
  Abatement.

  Ms. Elguira stated that currently the city is allocating $130,000.

  Arturo Cervantes, Director of Public Works does not have the exact
  amount but it's close to $450,000.

  Vice Mayor Hurtado asked if that amount does not include the $130,000.

  Mr. Cervantes stated that it includes the $130,000.

  Vice Mayor Hurtado asked if the city has any programs to educate people
  as to the negative impacts of graffiti. It seems the city spends over
  $100,000 every year.

  Mr. Cervantes stated the city does not have a graffiti abatement outreach.

  Vice Mayor Hurtado asked if the city penalizes anyone getting caught.

  Darren Arakawa, Chief of Police is not prepared to answer statistically
  what the consequences are. However, in years past when someone was
  arrested the judge would send a letter to the city asking how much the
  restitution would be.

  Page 3 of 12
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 25, 2023

1
COMMUNITY DEV/
HOUSING CONT'D  Council Member Rios stated that often it's the young people and we need
  to find a way to help them become good citizens.

  Mayor Avalos asked if the Affordable Housing Development is a new
  program.

  Ms. Elguira stated that it is to be determined. As the city receives
  proposals for affordable housing development then we can use this fund.

  Mayor Avalos stated that this project is for developers not for the
  community. She would prefer this item to be for first-time home buyers in
  the community.

  Ms. Elguira stated that we used to have the first-time home buyers'
  program. The city is still receiving revenue from the first-time home
  buyers that are paying off their loans, selling or refinancing.

  Chris Jeffers, City Manager stated that the program originally started
  through the Community Redevelopment program so the guidelines are
  much different than HUD. HUD is more restrictive.

  Vice Mayor Hurtado asked if a person qualifies for the first-time buyer
  program must they live in it or are they allowed to rent the home. Are they
  allowed to build an ADU?

  Mr. Jeffers stated that staff would need to check with HUD.

  Mayor Avalos requested a CDBG of $10,000 to help residents.

  Council Member Barron asked if this item can be approved with the
  recommendations from staff

  Council Member Davila asked from where are the $10,000 coming from.

  Mayor Avalos suggested $5,000 from Family Violence and $5,000 from
  Police Explorers.

  Council Member Davila disagrees. The city has provided enough money
  for Compatior. The council has yet to receive any information that was
  requested. She suggested moving with the staff's recommendations.

  Council Member Barrons agrees with Council Member Davila.

  Page 4 of 12
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 25, 2023

  COMMENTS FROM THE AUDIENCE
Am-,  NON-AGENDA ITEMS  Mario Dominguez, Jr. is requesting the Council speak with
  Congresswoman Nanette Barragan and Senator Lena Gonzalez to speak
  with Janice Hahn about the LA River project.

  Alex Cueto, designer for Art Design Services, is present tonight with a
  client. Mr. Cueto stated that in January 2022 the planning department for
  an ADU or any type of submittal was $231. Three months later it was
  $269. In August was $1,085. The City of South Gate is taking longer than
  any other city in the State of California to approve ADU's and the fees are
  higher.

  Juan Gonzalez has 50 years living in the City of South Gate and is
  complaining about street vendors.

  Vanessa Cruz from the Office of Congresswoman Barragan stating the
  congresswoman is holding a small business resource session on Monday,
  May 1, 2023, at 5:30 p.m. in the city of Paramount.

  Thomas Buckley stated receiving complaints from residents regarding
  encampments and trees being cut down between Hildreth and the pool.

  REPORT AND COMMENTS
  FROM CITY OFFICIALS  Meredith Elguira, Director of Community Development, responded to Mr.
  Cueto's statements stating that it is true the planning division is behind.
  There are two planners working on ADU's and that was prior increasing
  the fees last year. Five applications are being processed per week. The
  department was able to hire planning consultants. She also stated
  explaining to Mr. Cueto's son of the fees.

  Mayor Avalos asked Ms. Elguira how many planning consultations are
  checking the ADU's plans.

  Ms. Elguira stated there are two additional consultations.

  Ms. Elguira stated that the department is providing more notices of
  violations.

  Chris Jeffers, City Manager stated the Chief will follow up on the
  homeless issues. The trees were being worked on at the South Gate Park
  that are problematic. Vanessa from Congresswoman Barragan's Office
  called the City Manager's Office regarding the small business resource
  session, and it was posted on the City's website. The city is in discussions
  with the City's Prosecutor and staff on bringing a revised ordinance
  addressing vendors.

  Page 5 of 12
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 25, 2023

REPORT AND COMMENTS
FROM CITY OFFICIALS
CONT'D  Council Member Rios is concerned that the new tree vendor will be
  cutting down trees that provide shade.

  Arturo Cervantes, Director of Public Works stated that this year is the first
  cycle of the four-year tree trimming program. Some trees have been
  identified to be problematic.

  Council Member Barron had the pleasure of sitting on the Parks &
  Recreation Commission for about 5 years and stated that Glen Massey
  from the Parks Department loves trees. Mr. Massey will work with the
  arborist.

  Steve Costley, Acting Director of Parks & Recreation stated that
  Assemblymember Rendon is having a biking event this Saturday at
  Hollydale Regional Park and an earth day event. On May 5th we will be
  holding our next centennial event at the golf course area. The next
  Saturday will be the JAA opening day for the regular baseball season @
  10:00 a.m.

  Arturo Cervantes, Director of Public Works stated taking the first-year
  cycle trim for all the trees on the public right-of-way, trimmed over 2,800
  trees in the community and done removal and other treatments. On the fire
  hydrant flushing program, we have completed thirteen of the sixteen
  zones. We have flushed nearly 1,000 fire hydrants.

  Jon Hamilton, Director of Human Services reported on the positions the
  city is recruiting.

  Darren Arakawa, Police Chief highlighted upcoming community events.

  Kris Ryan, Director of Administrative Services stated that the city will be
  transitioning to a new phone system this Friday.

  Yodit Glaze, City Clerk stated that the passport services in the City Clerk's
  Office is opened for the public. She also stated that two hourly positions
  will be hired.

  Jose De La Paz, City Treasurer wished Vice Mayor Hurtado a Happy
  Birthday.

  Chris Jeffers, City Manager congratulated Public Works Department for an
  excellent job during earth day this past weekend.

  Raul F. Salinas, City Attorney had nothing to report at this time.

  Page 6 of 12
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 25, 2023

REPORT AND COMMENTS
FROM CITY OFFICIALS
CONT'D  Council Member Davila wished Vice Mayor Hurtado a Happy Birthday.
  She attended earth day which was very well attended. She commended
  Public Works Department for a job well done during earth day. She also
  attended Stanford Elementary School's Career Day and visited three
  classrooms. At the last city council meeting, she and Mayor Avalos were
  in Sacramento advocating for our city. The League of California Cities are
  working on housing and homelessness. The state is asking all cities to
  build eight thousand houses but there is no funding. The League of
  California is asking the state for three billion dollars for the housing. They
  did meet with the legislatures asking for an amendment on how many
  houses need to be built, especially in the city of South Gate. Another issue
  was homelessness.

  Council Member Davila attended a workshop on safety, and she spoke to
  City Manager about having an active shooter scenario. She stated that the
  City of Paramount had an active shooter scenario at Paramount High
  School. She asked to adjourn in memory of Cecilia Martinez wife of Ted
  Noudis (a long-time resident of South Gate and former business owner of
  T and C's Restaurant on Tweedy Blvd) who passed away this Sunday.

  Mayor Avalos stated that while they were at the capital there was an active
  shooter at the capital. The active shooter left the capital and then went to
  the city of Roseville where he was captured.

  Council Member Barron had the opportunity to attend Coffee with a Cop
  on April 13th. He is asking to get ahold of the local schools and ask if they
  are trained in using Automated External Defibrillator (AED). He informed
  Mr. Gonzalez that the city is working on updating the ordinance regarding
  vendors. He informed Mr. Cueto that he too built an ADU, and it is
  stressful and hopes there will be an improvement on the waiting list. He
  had the pleasure of meeting with the Community Development
  Department and thanked the director for setting up the meeting.

  Council Member Rios stated that the city of Bell Gardens improved their
  ordinance and made certain all vendors have licenses and permits. He
  stated that the active shooter topic was discussed at the college he works
  at. He had the pleasure of going to the International Studies Learning
  Center and hearing some of the senior projects. He too attended the Earth
  Day event. He will be attending on May 4th the Southern California
  Associates of Government and will be the delegate for the city. Also on
  May 4th is National Prayer Breakfast at South Gate Park.

  Vice Mayor Hurtado stated that the South Gate JAA will be having its
  opening day on Saturday, May 6th and everyone is invited to attend and
  Ken Landreaux the former baseball player for the Dodgers will be present.
  He too attended the Earth Day event. He received notifications of large

  Page 7 of 12
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 25, 2023

REPORT AND COMMENTS
FROM CITY OFFICIALS
CONT'D  gatherings at Hollydale Park without permits. He attended the Coffee with
  the Principal at South Gate Middle School and street vendors and
  homeless were brought up. He thanked everyone for the birthday wishes.

  Mayor Avalos attended the League of California Cities advocating for our
  community to bring in resources. One of the issues discussed was the
  building of homes and building up. She had the privilege of attending the
  Women's Club conference on May 17th and Stanford Elementary School's
  2nd Annual Career. She thanked Mr. Gonzalez for bringing up the vendor
  issues in the city. She understands the urgency of ADU's and hopes they
  can expedite the community members. She also attended The Wall Las
  Memorias conducted by Janice Hahn and Jackie Goldberg in the city of
  Bell. She also attended HUB Cities. She mentioned Compatior was
  honored to receive the mentored internship program grant which is a
  component of the California Department of Mental Health Services
  Behavior Health and Workhorse Department. Compatior is going to
  partner with Loyola Marymount, East LA College and LA Trade Tech to
  mentor students that are in the field of opioid addiction and substance use.

  Council Member Davila requested an update from staff regarding East LA
  College.

  Council Member Rios stated the college needs to vacate the building by
  June 24. The building across the street is expected to be built by the fall of
  next year.

CONSENT CALENDAR  Agenda Items 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 were approved by motion of Council
  Member Davila and seconded by Vice Mayor Avalos.
  ROLL CALL: Council Member Barron, yes; Council Member Davila,
  yes; Council Member Rios, yes; Vice Mayor Hurtado, yes (recused for
  Items 2 and 5); Mayor Avalos, yes.

2
STREETS/SIDEWALKS/
LANDSCAPING  The City Council made a finding and adopted Resolution No. 2023-21-
  CC entitled Resolution of the City Council of the City of South Gate, State
  of California, declaring an emergency still exists and authorizing repair,
  replacement or maintenance activities of public facilities related to the
  Urban Orchard Project, City Project No. 539-PRK, without public
  bidding, pursuant to the emergency contracting procedures of the South
  Gate Municipal Code and the California Public Contract Code, during
  Consent Calendar.

  Page 8 of 12
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF APRIL 25, 2023

  3
111  STREETS/SIDEWALKS/
  LANDSCAPING  The City Council unanimously approved A & B during Consent Calendar:

  a.  Resolution No. 2023-22-CC entitled Resolution of the City
  Council of the City of South Gate, California, preliminarily
  approving the Engineer's Report required for the proceedings of
  the Fiscal Year 2023/24 Annual Levy and Collection of
  Assessments for the Street Lighting and Landscape Maintenance
  District No. 1; and

  b.  Resolution No. 2023-23-CC entitled Resolution of the City
  Council of the City of South Gate, California, declaring the City's
